lead: A single-stage detector predicts boxes and class scores straight from the image in one forward pass. It does not propose regions first. YOLO cuts the image into a grid and lets each cell predict boxes; SSD predicts from feature maps at several scales; RetinaNet adds a loss that fixes the background imbalance. The speed makes these models common in live video, phone cameras, drones and CCTV, where a frame must be tagged before the next one arrives.
prereq: You need 6.4 for IoU, NMS and two-stage detection, and 6.3 for the convolutional backbone.

blocks.text: YOLO divides the input into an S × S grid. In the first version S = 7, so the image is 7 cells across and 7 down. Each cell predicts B bounding boxes; B = 2. A box has five numbers: x, y, w, h and confidence. x and y are the box centre offsets inside that cell, scaled from 0 to 1. w and h are the box width and height as fractions of the whole image. The cell also gives C class probabilities, one per class. On PASCAL VOC, C = 20.
Confidence is Pr(object) × IoU with the truth box. Pr(object) is 1 if the object centre lies in the cell and 0 otherwise. IoU is intersection over union, the overlap between predicted and true boxes.

blocks.where: B is the number of boxes per cell; C is the number of classes. Total numbers = S × S × (5B + C). With S = 7, B = 2 and C = 20, the tensor is 7 × 7 × 30 and holds 1470 numbers.

blocks.text: Only the cell whose area contains the object centre is responsible for that object. Other cells are trained as no-object. This stops many cells from claiming the same object.

At test time, for each box multiply confidence by the class probability. Drop boxes below a confidence threshold. Apply non-maximum suppression, NMS, at IoU 0.5. NMS keeps the top score and removes overlapping boxes of the same class.
The training loss adds box, confidence and class terms. λ_coord = 5 raises the box term. λ_noobj = 0.5 lowers the confidence term for empty cells, so the many empty cells do not dominate.

sections.h3: SSD: many feature maps, default boxes

blocks.text: SSD, Single Shot MultiBox Detector, also skips proposals. A base convolutional network produces a first feature map. Extra convolutional layers produce smaller maps: 38×38, 19×19, 10×10, 5×5, 3×3 and 1×1 in a common SSD300 design with 300×300 input. Each map cell predicts a fixed set of default boxes, also called anchor boxes. The boxes have several aspect ratios, such as 1:1, 2:1 and 1:2, and more than one scale.

At each location, for each default box, the network outputs 4 offsets and C + 1 scores. The extra score is background. A 38×38 map with 4 default boxes and C = 20 gives 38×38×4 = 5776 box predictions at that scale alone.

Most default boxes are background, so SSD uses hard negative mining: sort background boxes by loss, keep only about 3 negatives for every positive, about 3:1. Train with smooth L1 for offsets and softmax for scores. At test, threshold scores and run NMS.
Early large maps catch small objects. Late small maps catch large objects.
RetinaNet is one-stage with feature pyramids. Its problem is class imbalance: a dense detector may see 1 object and 100000 background boxes. Focal loss reduces the loss of easy examples.

blocks.where: p_t is the probability of the true class; γ = 2 focuses training on hard examples; α_t balances classes.

items: YOLOv2 adds anchor boxes and batch normalisation.
Later YOLO versions use stronger backbones and better augmentation.
Two-stage detectors such as Faster R-CNN are better on small objects and accuracy, but slower.
One-stage detectors are faster, simpler to train, and weaker on very small objects unless they use multi-scale maps.

figure.caption: One pass turns the 448×448 image into a 7×7×30 tensor with 1470 numbers and 98 boxes; the cell holding the dog's centre has 30 numbers (5B+C). That cell's dog score is 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72 before the confidence threshold and NMS.

spec.title: YOLO one pass
spec.aria: YOLO single pass: a 448 by 448 by 3 image goes through one forward pass to a 7 by 7 by 30 tensor holding 1470 numbers and 98 boxes; the cell with the dog centre has 30 numbers, its dog score is 0.8 times 0.9 equals 0.72, then thresholding and NMS give final boxes.

examples.question: YOLO runs with S = 7, B = 2 and C = 20 on a 448×448 input. (a) What is the depth of the output tensor? (b) How many numbers are in the tensor? (c) How many boxes does the grid predict? (d) A cell contains an object and its best box has IoU 0.8 with the truth. That box's confidence is 0.8. What is the test-time score for class dog if the cell's dog probability is 0.9?
steps: Total numbers = S × S × depth = 7 × 7 × 30 = 49 × 30 = 1470 numbers.
Total boxes = S × S × B = 7 × 7 × 2 = 49 × 2 = 98 boxes.
examples.answer: The tensor depth is 30, the tensor holds 1470 numbers, the grid predicts 98 boxes, and the dog score is 0.72.
examples.check:
S = 7
B = 2
C = 20
depth = 5 * B + C
total = S * S * depth
boxes = S * S * B
conf = 0.8
p_dog = 0.9
score = conf * p_dog
print(depth)
print(total)
print(boxes)
print(round(score, 2))

traps: The YOLO tensor depth is 5B + C, not 5 + B·C. With B = 2 and C = 20 the depth is 30, not 45.
x and y are offsets inside one cell; w and h are fractions of the full image. Mixing the two gives wrong boxes.
Only the cell holding the object centre is responsible for the object. Neighbouring cells stay no-object.
At test time use confidence × class probability, not confidence alone.
SSD scores are C + 1 because background is a class; hard negative mining keeps about 3 negatives per positive.

quiz.q: For YOLO with S = 7, B = 2 and C = 20, what is the output tensor shape?

quiz.a: Empty cells are many. A lower weight stops their confidence loss from dominating training.

quiz.q: A YOLO cell has confidence 0.6 and dog probability 0.5. What is the test score for dog?
Why does SSD predict from several feature maps?
quiz.a: Large early maps see small objects; small late maps see large objects. Multi-scale maps cover object sizes.

quiz.q: An SSD map is 38×38 and uses 4 default boxes per cell. How many box predictions are made at this scale?
What does focal loss do in RetinaNet?
quiz.a: It down-weights easy negative examples so hard examples drive training.

quiz.q: Give one reason a two-stage detector can beat a one-stage detector on small objects.
quiz.a: The proposal stage re-samples regions at high resolution, so a small object gets a second focused look; a dense grid may have too few pixels per small object.

quiz.q: What is NMS used for at detector test time?
quiz.a: It removes overlapping duplicate boxes, keeping the top-scoring box per class.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems deploy YOLO and SSD through TensorRT or NCNN on phones and Jetson boards. Anchor-free detectors such as FCOS and CenterNet remove default boxes. Search terms: focal loss, feature pyramid network, YOLOv8, SSD Lite, hard negative mining.
